body.statement: At \(P=P^{\diamond}\), the declared objects satisfy \(X_0=\{-1/2,1/2\}\), \(H=\{(-1/2,1/2),(1/2,-1/2)\}\), \(g=0\), \(A=1/2\), \(T=0\), and \(\nu_P=\tfrac12\delta_{-1/2}-\tfrac12\delta_{1/2}\). The obstacle endpoints are \(\ell_P(-1/2)=\ell_P(1/2)=-1/2\) and \(r_P(-1/2)=r_P(1/2)=1/2\), so \(\mathcal C_P=\{u:|u(-1/2)|\le1/2,\ |u(1/2)|\le1/2\}\) and \(\Theta(P)=[-1,1]\). For every such \(u\), the displayed schedules of \(Q_u^{\diamond}\) preserve \(P^{\diamond}\), satisfy \(|b_u^{\diamond}|\le1\), obey parallel trends on the baseline-treatment support and, because their period difference is \(u(X)\) at every dose, also obey the stronger all-\(I\) equality, have \(m_{Q_u^{\diamond}}=u\), and attain \(\theta(Q_u^{\diamond})=u(1/2)-u(-1/2)\). The endpoint assignment \(u(-1/2)=1/2,u(1/2)=-1/2\) gives \(b_u^{\diamond}=-1\) and \(\theta(Q_u^{\diamond})=-1\); reversing the two signs gives \(b_u^{\diamond}=1\) and \(\theta(Q_u^{\diamond})=1\). This is a heterogeneous two-point baseline design with both signs of treatment change, not the common-zero-baseline scalar design.
body.justification: The calculation makes the non-singleton frontier and its full-law attainment visible in the smallest genuinely heterogeneous-baseline design.
body.gap: The common-zero-baseline bounded-slope interval in de Chaisemartin et al. (2024) has one baseline and one scalar nuisance; this example has two baselines, opposite change signs, a signed objective, and distinct affine completions.
body.consumer: The worked law is a unit test for endpoint software and a transparent template for explaining support-driven partial identification in applications.
body.proof_tex:
At the two atoms of \(P^{\diamond}\),
\[
(X,Z)=(-1/2,1/2)\quad\text{and}\quad(X,Z)=(1/2,-1/2),
\]
each with probability \(1/2\).  Thus
\[
X_0=\{-1/2,1/2\},
\qquad
H=\{(-1/2,1/2),(1/2,-1/2)\}.
\]
Because \(Y_1=Y_2=0\), \(g=0\) and \(T=0\), while
\[
A=E|Z|=\frac12,
\qquad
\nu_P=\frac12\delta_{-1/2}-\frac12\delta_{1/2}.
\]
With \(K=L=M=1\), the local cone at either baseline is \([-1/2,1/2]\).  Propagating the other baseline's cone across distance one cannot tighten this interval.  Direct substitution in the obstacle formulas therefore gives
\[
\ell_P(-1/2)=\ell_P(1/2)=-\frac12,
\qquad
r_P(-1/2)=r_P(1/2)=\frac12.
\]
The largest possible difference between two values in these intervals is one, so the one-Lipschitz condition adds no restriction.  Hence
\[
\mathcal C_P=\{u:|u(-1/2)|\leq1/2, |u(1/2)|\leq1/2\}.
\]
For such \(u\),
\[
J_P(u)=\frac{u(-1/2)-u(1/2)}2,
\qquad
\frac{T-J_P(u)}A=u(1/2)-u(-1/2).
\]
Its attained range is \([-1,1]\), proving \(\Theta(P)=[-1,1]\).

The displayed slope equals
\[
b_u^{\diamond}=
\begin{cases}
-2u(-1/2),&X=-1/2,\\
2u(1/2),&X=1/2,
\end{cases}
\]
and therefore \(|b_u^{\diamond}|\leq1\).  Evaluation at \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) gives the two observed zeros, so the complete observed law is preserved.  For every \(d\in[-1,1]\), direct subtraction gives
\[
Y_2^{Q_u^{\diamond}}(d)-Y_1^{Q_u^{\diamond}}(d)=u(X).
\]
Thus parallel trends holds conditionally on \((X,Z)\) and on \(X\), both on the baseline support and on all of \(I\), and \(m_{Q_u^{\diamond}}=u\).  The movement is \(b_u^{\diamond}Z=-u(X)\), so its magnitude is at most \(|Z|\); all legal restrictions follow.  The target is the value computed above.  If \(u(-1/2)=1/2\) and \(u(1/2)=-1/2\), then \(b_u^{\diamond}=-1\) at both atoms and \(\theta=-1\).  Reversing the signs gives \(b_u^{\diamond}=1\) and \(\theta=1\).  Both signs of treatment change and both baseline values are used, so this is not a common-baseline scalar design.
